concepts.topicTitle: Neurons, Synapses, and Neuromuscular Signal Transmission
concepts.label: Why Living Things Need Control and Coordination
concepts.cardText: We link visible movement with life because movement is a response to a change in the environment of the organism, and an attempt to use such changes to its advantage. This movement is carefully controlled: each kind of change evokes an appropriate movement, so we whisper rather than shout when talking in class. The movement made must depend on the event that triggers it, so it must be connected to the recognition of events in the environment, followed by only the correct response. Living organisms must therefore use systems providing control and coordination, and in multicellular organisms specialised tissues provide them.

concepts.topicTitle: Neurons, Synapses, and Neuromuscular Signal Transmission
concepts.label: Receptors and the Path of a Nerve Impulse
concepts.cardText: In animals, control and coordination are provided by nervous and muscular tissues. Information from the environment is detected by the specialised tips of some nerve cells, the receptors, usually located in sense organs such as the inner ear, nose and tongue. Gustatory receptors detect taste while olfactory receptors detect smell. The information, acquired at the end of the dendritic tip of a nerve cell, sets off a chemical reaction that creates an electrical impulse. It travels from the dendrite to the cell body, then along the axon to its end, where it sets off the release of chemicals that cross the gap, or synapse, and start a similar impulse in a dendrite of the next neuron.

concepts.topicTitle: Neurons, Synapses, and Neuromuscular Signal Transmission
concepts.label: How Muscles Move When a Nerve Impulse Arrives
concepts.cardText: When an action or movement is to be performed, muscle tissue does the final job. When a nerve impulse reaches a muscle, the muscle fibre must move. The simplest notion of movement at the cellular level is that muscle cells move by changing their shape so that they shorten. The answer lies in the chemistry of cellular components: muscle cells have special proteins that change both their shape and their arrangement in the cell in response to nervous electrical impulses. When this happens, the new arrangements of these proteins give the muscle cells a shorter form.

concepts.label: Reflex Action and the Reflex Arc
concepts.cardText: A reflex is something we do without thinking about it or without feeling in control of our reactions, as when we pull a hand back from a flame. Thinking is a complex activity involving many nerve impulses from many neurons, and it may take enough time for us to get burnt. So the body connects the nerve that detects heat to the nerve that moves muscles in a simpler way; such a connection is called a reflex arc. Reflex arcs are formed in the spinal cord itself, where nerves from all over the body meet in a bundle on their way to the brain, although the information input also goes on to reach the brain. Reflex arcs evolved because the thinking process of the brain is not fast enough, and they continue to be more efficient for quick responses.

concepts.topicTitle: Structure and Functions of the Human Brain and Central Nervous System
concepts.label: The Brain, Spinal Cord and Nervous System
concepts.cardText: The spinal cord is made of nerves which supply information to think about. Thinking involves more complex mechanisms and neural connections, concentrated in the brain, the main coordinating centre of the body. The brain and spinal cord constitute the central nervous system; they receive information from all parts of the body and integrate it. Voluntary actions such as writing, talking or moving a chair are based on deciding what to do next, so the brain also sends messages to muscles. The communication between the central nervous system and other parts of the body is facilitated by the peripheral nervous system, which consists of cranial nerves arising from the brain and spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord.

concepts.topicTitle: Structure and Functions of the Human Brain and Central Nervous System
concepts.label: Parts of the Brain and What Each Controls
concepts.cardText: The brain has three major parts or regions: the fore-brain, mid-brain and hind-brain. The fore-brain is the main thinking part. It has regions which receive sensory impulses from receptors, with separate areas specialised for hearing, smell and sight, and areas of association where the information is interpreted by putting it together with other information. A decision is then passed to the motor areas which control voluntary muscles. The feeling of being full comes from a hunger centre in a separate part of the fore-brain. Involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting are controlled by the medulla in the hind-brain. The cerebellum, also in the hind-brain, is responsible for precision of voluntary actions and maintaining posture and balance.

concepts.label: How the Brain and Spinal Cord Are Protected
concepts.cardText: A delicate organ like the brain, which is so important for a variety of activities, needs to be carefully protected. The body is designed so that the brain sits inside a bony box, the skull. Inside the box, the brain is contained in a fluid-filled balloon which provides further shock absorption. If you run your hand down the middle of your back, you feel a hard, bumpy structure: the vertebral column or backbone, which protects the spinal cord.

concepts.topicTitle: Immediate Non-Growth Movements and Plant Tropisms
concepts.label: How Plants Respond to Touch Without Nerves
concepts.cardText: Plants have neither a nervous system nor muscles, yet the leaves of the sensitive plant fold up and droop quickly when touched. The movement happens at a point different from the point of touch, so information that a touch has occurred must be communicated. Plants use electrical-chemical means to convey this information from cell to cell, but unlike animals they have no specialised tissue for conducting information. Some cells must change shape for movement to happen: instead of the special proteins of animal muscle cells, plant cells change shape by changing the amount of water in them, swelling or shrinking. There is no growth involved in this movement.

concepts.topicTitle: Immediate Non-Growth Movements and Plant Tropisms
concepts.label: Growth Movements of Plants: Tropisms
concepts.cardText: Plants show two different types of movement: one dependent on growth and the other independent of growth. The directional movement of a seedling is caused by growth, and if it is prevented from growing it will not move. Environmental triggers such as light or gravity change the directions in which plant parts grow; these directional, or tropic, movements can be towards the stimulus or away from it. In phototropism, shoots bend towards light while roots bend away from it. In geotropism, roots grow downwards and shoots usually grow upwards, away from the earth. An example of chemotropism is the growth of pollen tubes towards ovules. Tendrils circle a support because the part in contact grows less rapidly than the part away from it.

concepts.label: Why Cells Also Use Chemical Communication
concepts.cardText: Fast responses need quick information transfer, and electrical impulses are an excellent means for this. But they have limits. First, they reach only those cells that are connected by nervous tissue, not each and every cell. Second, after an impulse is generated and transmitted, the cell takes some time to reset its mechanisms, so cells cannot continually create and transmit impulses. Most multicellular organisms therefore also use chemical communication: stimulated cells release a chemical compound that diffuses all around, and cells with special molecules on their surfaces detect it. This is slower, but it can reach all cells of the body regardless of nervous connections, steadily and persistently.

concepts.label: Plant Hormones: Auxin, Gibberellins, Cytokinins and Abscisic Acid
concepts.cardText: Different plant hormones coordinate growth, development and responses to the environment. They are synthesised at places away from where they act and simply diffuse to the area of action. When growing plants detect light, auxin, synthesised at the shoot tip, helps the cells to grow longer. When light comes from one side, auxin diffuses towards the shady side of the shoot, and this concentration stimulates the cells on the side away from light to grow longer, so the plant appears to bend towards light. Gibberellins, like auxins, help in the growth of the stem. Cytokinins promote cell division and are in greater concentration in fruits and seeds. Abscisic acid inhibits growth, and its effects include wilting of leaves.

concepts.topicTitle: Animal Hormones, the Endocrine System and Feedback Mechanisms
concepts.label: Adrenaline and the Body's Emergency Response
concepts.cardText: When an animal such as a squirrel is in a scary situation, its body must prepare for fighting or running away, using a great deal of energy in controlled ways. If the body relied only on electrical impulses, the range of tissues instructed to prepare would be limited. A chemical signal reaches all cells of the body and provides the wide-ranging changes needed. This is done using the hormone adrenaline, secreted from the adrenal glands directly into the blood and carried to different parts of the body. The heart beats faster, supplying more oxygen to muscles. Blood to the digestive system and skin is reduced by contraction of muscles around small arteries, diverting blood to the skeletal muscles. The breathing rate also increases. Animal hormones are part of the endocrine system, a second way of control and coordination.

concepts.topicTitle: Animal Hormones, the Endocrine System and Feedback Mechanisms
concepts.label: Hormones for Coordinated Growth: Thyroxin, Growth Hormone, Sex Hormones and Insulin
concepts.cardText: Even in animal bodies growth happens in carefully controlled places, and hormones help. Iodine is necessary for the thyroid gland to make thyroxin, which regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism so as to provide the best balance for growth; a deficiency of iodine can cause goitre, with a swollen neck, which is why iodised salt is advised. Growth hormone, secreted by the pituitary, regulates growth and development; its deficiency in childhood leads to dwarfism. The changes of puberty are due to testosterone in males and oestrogen in females. Insulin, produced by the pancreas, helps regulate blood sugar levels; if it is not secreted in proper amounts, blood sugar rises, which is why some diabetics are treated with insulin injections.

concepts.topicTitle: Animal Hormones, the Endocrine System and Feedback Mechanisms
concepts.label: Feedback Mechanisms and the Summary of Control and Coordination
concepts.cardText: Because hormones must be secreted in precise quantities, the timing and amount of hormone released are regulated by feedback mechanisms. For example, if the sugar levels in blood rise, they are detected by the cells of the pancreas, which respond by producing more insulin. As the blood sugar level falls, insulin secretion is reduced. In summary, control and coordination are the functions of the nervous system and hormones. The responses of the nervous system can be classified as reflex action, voluntary action or involuntary action, using electrical impulses and acting through muscles. Chemical coordination is seen in both plants and animals, hormones moving from one part of an organism to another, and a feedback mechanism regulates their action.
